notes: Ruling slot 13: Macías's 1968 vehicle IPGE as the 1 Jan 1970 entry, with PUNT (founded 1970 as the single party under Macías, renamed PUNT in 1971) as second period from 1970.7.7. MD's PDGE (1987) is anachronistic and not used. MUNGE and MONALIGE are effectively crushed after the March 1969 crisis (Ondó Edú and Atanasio Ndongo killed). Unión Bubi in slot 0 as the pro-Spanish autonomist force.

0.name: Unión Bubi
0.text:
The Bubi Union represents the Bubi, the original people of Fernando Poo, who feared domination by the Fang majority of Río Muni and sought separate status for the island. Its leader Edmundo Bosio Dioco backed Macías in the 1968 run-off and has been co-opted into his government.

The party favours autonomy for Fernando Poo, protection of Bubi land, close ties with Spain and the cocoa economy built under Spanish rule. Its leverage lies in the island's wealth and in its role as the voice of a distinct people, though Macías's growing suspicion of the Bubi leaves it ever more exposed.

1.name: Movimiento de Unión Nacional de Guinea Ecuatorial
1.english: National Union Movement of Equatorial Guinea
1.native_full: Movimiento de Unión Nacional de Guinea Ecuatorial
1.text:
MUNGE was the party of Bonifacio Ondó Edú, head of the autonomous government from 1964 and Macías's main rival in the 1968 presidential election. After his defeat Ondó Edú fled to Gabon, was handed back and killed in 1969; the movement is now leaderless and persecuted.

Its surviving supporters stand for a gradual, orderly independence in close partnership with Spain, Catholic values, private property and the authority of educated Fang notables. Their base lies among Río Muni's mission-educated elite and cocoa farmers, but fear of the regime has driven most of them into silence or exile.

2.name: Unión Democrática Fernandina
2.text:
The Fernandino Democratic Union speaks for the Fernandinos, the English- and Spanish-speaking Creole families of Santa Isabel descended from freed slaves and West African settlers. Educated, Protestant or Catholic and long prosperous through cocoa, they formed a party to defend their place at the 1967-1968 constitutional talks.

The Union favours constitutional government, individual rights, free trade and the rule of law, and fears both Fang dominance and arbitrary rule. Its leverage lies in property, education and business skills in Santa Isabel, but its small numbers make it vulnerable to Macías's suspicion of the old elites.

3.name: Los Exiliados de Madrid
3.text:
Since the crisis of March 1969, when Spanish troops and settlers left and Macías purged his rivals, a growing number of Guinean students, civil servants and professionals have taken refuge in Madrid and Barcelona. They form loose committees of exiles who meet in cafés and student residences.

The exiles call for the restoration of the 1968 constitution, free elections, trade-union rights and a welfare state financed by cocoa and timber. They seek the support of Spanish democrats and European socialists. Their leverage is limited to information and propaganda abroad, while Franco's government forbids reporting on Guinea.

4.name: Los Becarios de Moscú
4.text:
As Macías turns away from Spain, Equatorial Guinea opens relations with the Soviet Union and Cuba, and young Guineans are sent to study at the Patrice Lumumba University in Moscow and other Soviet-bloc schools. A small cadre of returning graduates sees itself as the vanguard of a future socialist state.

They advocate nationalisation of the cocoa plantations, a Leninist party, close alignment with the Soviet bloc and Soviet fishing and naval cooperation. Their leverage lies in their technical training and in Macías's need for Eastern allies, though the president tolerates no rival authority.

5.name: Los Radicales de Bata
5.text:
In Bata, the main town of Río Muni, a small circle of young teachers and secondary-school graduates, inspired by Sékou Touré, Nkrumah and the Cuban revolution, demands a revolution deeper than Macías's personal rule. Many studied in Spain, where they encountered the anti-Franco student movement.

They call for land reform, the end of all Spanish economic influence, popular assemblies and pan-African revolution. They are critical of the cult of the president but share his anti-colonial rhetoric. Their leverage is limited to schools and youth groups, where their ideas spread quietly despite growing surveillance.

6.name: Los Ancianos del Abaa
6.text:
In the villages of Río Muni, Fang elders meet in the abaa, the men's council house that is the heart of clan life. Many see independence as the chance to cast off Spanish missionaries, colonial law and the Western habits of the educated elite.

The elders stand for Fang custom, clan authority, polygamy, ancestral religion and hostility to Spain and the Catholic Church, sympathising with Macías's anti-Western rhetoric. Their leverage lies in the villages of the mainland, where the abaa still settles disputes and mobilises support for whoever respects its authority.

7.name: El Clan de Mongomo
7.text:
President Macías relies above all on his relatives and fellow Esangui clansmen from the Mongomo district of Río Muni. They fill the key posts in the National Guard, the police and the prisons; his nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema is among the officers rising through the security apparatus.

The clan has no ideology beyond the preservation of its power, embracing anti-Spanish and anti-Western rhetoric and courting the Soviet bloc for arms and support. Its leverage is total control of the means of coercion, which makes it the real backbone of the regime and its most likely successor.

8.name: Los Comerciantes libaneses de Bata
8.text:
A handful of Lebanese families, part of the Shia trading diaspora spread from Dakar to Douala, run shops and import businesses in Bata and Santa Isabel. They took over some trade abandoned by Spanish merchants in 1969, and their notables follow the revival of Imam Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon.

They favour a modern Shia identity, community schools and cautious accommodation with whoever rules. They have no political ambitions but considerable economic weight: credit, imports and trade links with Cameroon and Gabon that the shrinking Guinean economy increasingly depends on.

9.name: El Círculo de Tiro
9.text:
Among the small Lebanese community of Bata and Santa Isabel, a few devout young men educated in the religious schools of Tyre maintain links with the seminaries of Najaf. They gather for prayers and religious lessons in private homes.

They preach strict observance, the authority of the senior clergy and a rejection of both Western and Marxist materialism, seeing Shia Islam as a complete social order. Their numbers are tiny and their influence is confined to family networks, but they keep the community's religious identity alive far from home.

10.name: Los Imanes de Santa Isabel
10.text:
Equatorial Guinea's Muslims are mainly Hausa and other West African traders and workers living in Santa Isabel and Bata, many of them arrived via Nigeria and Cameroon. Their imams lead modest prayer houses and represent the community before the authorities.

They practise a conservative Maliki Sunni Islam, avoid politics and seek protection for their trade and worship under an increasingly unpredictable regime. Their leverage lies in their role in small trade and transport, and in their links to the wider Muslim networks of Nigeria and Cameroon.

11.name: La Senda de Sokoto
11.text:
Among Hausa traders and migrant workers in Santa Isabel, itinerant preachers from northern Nigeria recall the Sokoto Caliphate and Usman dan Fodio's jihad. Their small circle meets outside the established prayer houses.

They preach that Muslims must live under sharia and a restored caliphate, condemning the Christian and secular order around them and the compromises of the established imams. They have no arms and very few followers, but their message finds an audience among poor migrants who feel abused and unprotected in a hostile land.

12.name: Los Antiguos de Al-Azhar
12.text:
A few Muslim teachers from Nigeria and Cameroon who studied at Al-Azhar in Cairo serve the small Muslim communities of Santa Isabel and Bata. In Cairo they encountered the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood, which they bring to their Qur'anic classes.

They promote modern Islamic education, Arabic literacy, mutual aid and moral renewal, presenting Islam as an answer to colonial Christianity and to dictatorship. Their influence is limited to teaching and community associations, but they give the Muslim minority a more organised voice.

13.name: Idea Popular de Guinea Ecuatorial
13.text:
IPGE, a radical Fang nationalist movement founded in the late 1950s, formed the core of the coalition that carried Francisco Macías Nguema to the presidency in the 1968 independence elections. Since the March 1969 crisis and the flight of the Spanish, Macías rules by decree and IPGE serves as the network of his loyalists.

It preaches anti-colonial nationalism, the primacy of the Fang mainland, African socialism and non-alignment, while turning toward the Soviet bloc, Cuba and China. Its leverage is the presidency itself: Macías dominates government, the National Guard and the youth militias.

13.name: Partido Único Nacional de los Trabajadores
13.native_full: Partido Único Nacional de los Trabajadores
13.text:
PUNT is the single party created by President Francisco Macías Nguema in 1970, absorbing all existing parties into one national organisation. It is the instrument of the president's personal rule, organising mass rallies, youth militias and the cult of the 'Unique Miracle' of Equatorial Guinea.

It proclaims anti-colonial nationalism, workers' unity and non-alignment, while aligning more and more with the Soviet bloc, Cuba and China. Membership is compulsory for public life. Its leverage is total: dissent means prison, exile or death, and the party controls every office, school and village of the country.

14.name: Iglesia católica en Guinea Ecuatorial
14.text:
The Catholic Church, built by Claretian missionaries over a century of Spanish rule, is the faith of most Equatorial Guineans and runs many of the country's schools. Rafael María Nze Abuy, Bishop of Bata, is the first Guinean bishop, alongside the Spanish-led diocese of Santa Isabel.

The Church defends Christian education, family values and religious freedom, and quietly opposes the arbitrary rule and anti-clericalism of the regime, without siding with Madrid or any bloc. Its leverage lies in the loyalty of the faithful, its schools and its international links to Rome and Spain.

15.name: Cámara Agrícola de Fernando Poo
15.native_full: Cámara Oficial Agrícola de Fernando Poo
15.text:
The Agricultural Chamber of Fernando Po represents the cocoa and coffee planters of the island, mostly Spanish, whose plantations made Guinea one of Africa's richest colonies. After the crisis of 1969, most Spanish planters fled, but the chamber still speaks for the remaining estates and their Fernandino partners.

It demands security for property, the return of Nigerian contract labour, preferential access to the Spanish market and protection from confiscation. Its leverage lies in the cocoa trade, still the main source of foreign currency, though Macías's hostility is quickly eroding the plantations' value.

16.name: Los Cacaoteros Fernandinos
16.text:
Alongside the large Spanish estates, Fernandino and Bubi smallholders, traders and transporters form a native middle class around the cocoa economy of Fernando Poo. With the Spanish gone, they hope to take over plantations and trade on their own account.

They want free markets, secure land titles, low taxes and freedom from state requisitions and political extortion. They distrust both Spanish monopolies and Macías's arbitrary regime. Their leverage lies in their commercial skills and land, which the regime needs to keep the cocoa economy running.

17.name: Los Guardianes del Pico Basilé
17.text:
On Fernando Poo, a few Guinean foresters and teachers trained under the Spanish forestry service watch over the cloud forests of Pico Basilé and the island's south, home to rare monkeys and nesting sea turtles. They fear for the forests as timber companies and charcoal burners advance.

They call for protected reserves, controls on logging and hunting and the preservation of the island's unique wildlife for future generations. Their political weight is negligible, but their technical expertise and the support of the island's naturalists make them the only voice for nature in the young republic.

18.name: Movimiento Nacional de Liberación de la Guinea Ecuatorial
18.english: National Liberation Movement of Equatorial Guinea
18.native_full: Movimiento Nacional de Liberación de la Guinea Ecuatorial
18.text:
MONALIGE was the main independence movement, formed in exile with support from Ghana and Guinea and led by Atanasio Ndongo Miyone. After Ndongo, Macías's foreign minister, was killed following the alleged coup attempt of March 1969, the movement was purged; its survivors hide in Río Muni or live in exile.

It stands for pan-African socialism, a democratic constitution, land for peasants and non-alignment in the tradition of Nkrumah and Sékou Touré. Its leverage lies in its legacy as the movement of independence and in networks of militants among teachers and the youth of Río Muni.

19.name: La Línea de Pekín
19.text:
As Equatorial Guinea seeks new partners, a few young cadres in the presidency and the youth movement look to China rather than Moscow, inspired by the Cultural Revolution and by Chinese aid elsewhere in Africa. They read Mao's works in Spanish translation and admire peasant mobilisation.

They call for collective farming, mass campaigns, self-reliance and independence from both superpowers, criticising Soviet influence as a new imperialism. Their leverage is small, but they have the ear of officials eager for Chinese aid, and Peking's diplomacy is actively seeking new friends in Central Africa.

20.name: Guinea para los Guineanos
20.text:
Resentment against foreigners runs high in Equatorial Guinea: against the Spanish who dominated the colony, and against the tens of thousands of Nigerian contract workers on the cocoa plantations of Fernando Poo. This populist mood is stoked by the regime's speeches and its youth activists.

It demands the expulsion of foreigners, the Africanisation of all property and jobs, and vengeance against those who served the colonial order. It has no formal leadership, but its slogans fill the president's rallies and give the regime a ready mob against Spaniards, Nigerians and educated Guineans alike.

21.name: Las Milicias de Macías
21.text:
Since the March 1969 crisis, young militants loyal to the president have formed armed groups that patrol the streets of Santa Isabel and Bata, hunting 'traitors', searching homes and enforcing the cult of Macías. They operate alongside the National Guard and answer to the president's inner circle.

They embrace a fanatical nationalism, the deification of the leader, hatred of Spain, intellectuals and the Church, and violence as a tool of politics. Their leverage lies in terror: they make any open dissent fatal and can be turned against any group the president suspects of disloyalty.

22.name: Guardia Nacional
22.text:
The National Guard, successor to the colonial Territorial Guard, is the young republic's only armed force. Since the Spanish Civil Guard withdrew in 1969, it has been commanded by Guinean officers trained in Spain's military academies, increasingly chosen for their loyalty to Macías and his clan.

The officer corps values order, national unity and its own status, and is wary of the president's unpredictable purges. It is small and poorly equipped, but as the only organised armed body it holds the key to the regime's survival, and any change of power will pass through its barracks.

23.name: Los Herederos de Moka
23.text:
Moka, the great Bubi king of the nineteenth century, unified the clans of Fernando Poo and resisted Spanish penetration of the interior. The Bubi kingship lost its power under colonial rule, but chiefly lineages in the island's highland villages still honour his memory and preserve the royal traditions.

The heirs stand for Bubi identity, customary land rights, the authority of traditional chiefs and the island's distinct destiny apart from Río Muni. Their leverage is cultural and symbolic, rooted in the loyalty of Bubi villages and the dream of a restored island kingdom.
